claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can initially be prepared in a high-temperature single-phase BCC state.
Rapid cooling of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 increases its density of non-equilibrium lattice defects relative to slow cooling.
Controlled severe plastic deformation increases dislocation density and grain-boundary density in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Rapid cooling or SPD promotes metastable secondary-phase formation during cooling or subsequent annealing.
Increased defect density lowers the nucleation barrier for metastable phases.
Dislocations and grain boundaries act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for metastable phases in this alloy.
The secondary phases generated by the proposed treatment may include a second BCC phase or an incipient HCP phase.
An SPD-processed HfNbTiZr alloy initially having a single BCC structure decomposed into two BCC phases during annealing, with an additional HCP phase at high strain.
Temperature-dependent formation and dissolution of metastable phases occurs in other compositionally complex alloys.
The defect-assisted mechanism should operate during and after cooling at temperatures up to about 1000 K, where atomic mobility permits nucleation without full equilibration.
High cooling rates or moderate SPD levels are sufficient to activate defect-assisted metastable-phase development.
A slow-cooled, undeformed Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 baseline should remain predominantly BCC with minimal secondary-phase formation.
Rapidly cooled or SPD-treated samples should have a higher metastable-secondary-phase volume fraction than the slow-cooled baseline.
Rapidly cooled or SPD-treated samples should have a finer dispersion of metastable secondary phases than the slow-cooled baseline.
The predicted phase changes may be accompanied by changes in hardness or other mechanical properties.
The mechanism becomes significant only above a critical defect-density threshold.
Very low defect densities or full high-temperature equilibration should suppress the proposed metastable-phase pathway.
XRD and TEM can be used to identify and quantify phase fractions, while TEM can assess dislocation density.
Failure of the treated samples to show a statistically significant increase in defect density or metastable-phase development relative to the baseline is proposed as falsification.
